passages.text: About This Article To use a sharpening stone, also known as a whetstone, first soak your stone in water or honing oil for 45 minutes. Then, lay a cloth over a cutting board and set the stone on top so that it lays out the long way in front of you. Set the heel of your knife on the edge furthest from you at the top, and tilt the blade up to a 15-degree angle. Keep your dominant hand on the handle with your index finger pushing down on top of the blade, and your nondominant hand on top of the blade near the tip. Using a firm and even amount of pressure, slowly drag the knife over the edge of the stone while moving the knife towards you so that the entire edge of the blade rubs against the stone. Do this 20-30 times depending on how dull your knife is. Then, flip the blade over and sharpen the other side. Finally, wash your knife and dry it with a towel to remove any grit and residue. passages.text: If you’ve ever struggled to cut vegetables cleanly or slice meat smoothly, chances are your knife needs sharpening. A dull knife not only makes cooking harder, but it’s also dangerous—blunt blades slip easily and can cause accidents. Sharpening your knife with a whetstone is one of the best ways to restore its cutting power. This guide shows you exactly how to use a whetstone safely, step-by-step. Whether you’re a kitchen beginner or a home chef, you’ll learn how to master this useful skill, avoid common mistakes, and keep your knives sharper for longer. What Is A Whetstone And Why Use One? A whetstone is a rectangular block made from natural or synthetic materials. Its rough surface grinds away metal from the knife’s edge, making it sharp again. Whetstones come in different grits—think of grit as the level of roughness. Lower grit (like 400) removes more metal and is good for repairing very dull knives. Higher grit (like 1000 or 3000) is used for finishing and polishing. Why use a whetstone instead of other sharpening tools? Unlike electric sharpeners or rods, whetstones let you control the sharpening angle and pressure. This helps protect your knife’s shape and extends its life. Most

Once you’ve prepared the stone and found your angle, the next (and possibly most important) step in getting a razor sharp knife is to re-define the edge. To do this you’re going to want to use the coarsest stone you have (use your 1,000 grit side). Find your angle and begin the back and forth motion. You will only be applying pressure when you pull the knife back — applying pressure in the forward stroke can damage your stone and mess with the edge. Make sure to apply a sizeable amount of pressure. Stand up and put some weight into it if you need to. You’ll want to work in one inch sections for your first time — it’s much easier to keep a consistent angle this way.
